chunks.content:
MAKING YOUR GAMES TIME BASED
In nearly all game engines, the frame rate varies quite a bit throughout gameplay
as the engine endeavors to display new frames as quickly as possible while your
computer is also doing dozens of other tasks. If the movement in a game is frame-
based, these variances in the frame rate will affect your game, with the motion
speeding up when the frame rate is higher and slowing down when it's lower. On
the other hand, when the movement in a game is time-based, objects will move at
a consistent speed regardless of the frame rate at which the game is running. To
achieve this, we can use TiPe.deltaTiPe, a built-in Unity field that updates each
frame and tells us the number of seconds that have passed since the last frame.
TiPe.deltaTiPe is usually very small. For a game running at 25 fps (frames per
second), TiPe.deltaTiPe is 0.04f, meaning that each frame takes 4/100 of a sec-
ond to display. If the // c line of code were run when the frame rate was 25 fps,
the code would resolve like this:
pos.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
pos.x += 1.0f * .f;
pos.x += 0.04f;
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
You might be wondering why lines // b through // d that you added to the
$ppleTree.8pdate() method were three lines instead of just one. Why couldn't
the code just be this?
transform.position.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
The answer is that transforP.position is a property, a method that is masquerad-
ing as a field (i.e., a function masquerading as a variable) through the use of get^}
and set^} accessors (see Chapter 26, "Classes"). Although getting (i.e., reading) the
value of a property's subcomponent is possible, setting a subcomponent of a property
is not possible. In other words, transforP.position.[ can be read, but it cannot be
set directly. This necessitates the creation of the temporary 9ector pos that can be
modified and then assigned back to transforP.position.
2. Save the script, return to Unity, and press Play.
When you click the Play button, you'll notice that the AppleTree moves very slowly. Try
some different values for speed in the AppleTree Inspector and see what feels good to
you. I set speed to 10, which makes it move at 10m/s (10 meters per second or 10 Unity
units per second).
So, in 1/25 of a second, pos.[ would increase by 0.04m per frame. Over the
course of a full second, pos.[ would increase by 0.04m per frame * 25 frames, for
a total of 1 meter in 1 second.
If instead the game were running at 100 fps, it would resolve as follows:
pos.x += speed * Time.deltaTime;
pos.x += 1.0f * .1f;
pos.x += 0.01f;
So, in 1/100 of a second, pos.[ would increase by 0.01m per frame. Over the
course of a full second, pos.[ would increase by 0.01m per frame * 100 frames,
for a total of 1 meter in 1 second.

MISSION DEMOLITION
Physics games are some of the most popular
around, making games like Angry Birds
household names. In this chapter, you make

Angry Birds and all the other physics games that
came before it, such as Crossbows and Catapults,

What You Will Learn
As the first in our series of tutorials, you'll learn several new concepts and review some
from Part II of the book, including:
■ Using vector math to fire a projectile
■ Importing pixel art assets from a UnityPackage (the clouds)
■ Working with prefabs and nested prefabs to make complex but changeable
GameObjects
■ Using the LineRenderer component to draw configurable trails for objects
■ Tracking and loading multiple levels
■ Using buttons in the uGUI user interface system
■ Converting a Collider to a trigger for sensing the end of a level
Figure 30.1 Mission Demolition as it will be at the end of this chapter
The Mission Demolition Prototype
This game is a simple version of a style of physics-based game that has been very
popular for decades. In our version, the player can launch a projectile from the slingshot
on the left at the castle on the right, with the goal of the projectile touching the green
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

goal box. We'll make a few different models of castle and will write code for managing
the camera view, keeping track of levels and the number of shots taken, randomizing
cloud positions, and implementing a line that tracks the projectile and shows where the
player's previous shots have gone.
Getting Started: Mission Demolition
Because this is the second prototype and you now have some experience under your
belt, this chapter is going to move a bit faster than the previous one when covering
things that you have already experienced. Of course, I still cover new topics in detail.

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. If
you need a refresher on the standard project setup procedure, see Appendix A,

Game Prototype Concept
In this game, the player uses a slingshot to fire projectiles at a castle, hoping to demolish
it. Each castle has a goal area that the projectile must touch for the player to continue to
the next level.
This is the desired sequence of events:
1. When the player's mouse pointer is in range of the slingshot, the slingshot should
glow.
2. If the player presses the left mouse button (mouse button 0 in Unity) down while the
slingshot is glowing, a projectile will instantiate at the location of the mouse pointer.
3. As the player moves and drags the mouse around with the button held down, the
projectile follows it, yet remains within a specific distance of the slingshot.

target area inside.
7. The player has a total of three shots to hit the goal. The most recent shot will leave a
trail so that the player can better judge their next shot.
Many of the preceding events relate to mechanics, but one is exclusively aesthetics:
step 4. All the other elements that mention art use that art for the purpose of game
mechanics, but step 4 is just to make the game look nicer, so it's less critical to the pro-
totype. When you're writing down your concepts for games, this is an important thing
to keep in mind. That isn't to say that you shouldn't implement things that are entirely
aesthetics in a prototype; you just need to be aware of and prioritize the elements that
will have the most direct impact on the game mechanics. For the sake of time and space,
this prototype focuses on the other elements, and I leave the implementation of step 4
for you to tackle later.

696 CHAPTER 30 MISSION DEMOLITION
In this example, you will set proMectilePrefab (a reference to the
GameObject prefab for all the projectiles) in the Unity Inspector before
running the game, whereas all the other fields will be set dynamically by code
while the game is running. The headers allow you to easily see the difference
between these in the Inspector.
b. Looking now at the other new fields:
■ launchPos stores the 3D world position of launchPoint.
■ proMectile is a reference to the new Projectile instance that is created.
■ aiPingMode is normally false, but is set to true when the player presses
mouse button 0 down over Slingshot. This state variable lets the rest of the
code know how to behave. In the next section, we'll write code for Sling-
shot's 8pdate() that only runs when aiPingMode true.
c. In $ZaNe(), we've added a single line to set launchPos.
d. The 2nMouseDoZn() method contains the bulk of changes for this listing.
e. It's worth noting here that if there is no Rigidbody component attached to the
Projectile prefab, this line will cause Unity to experience a red, NullReference-
Exception error. This would be because the Get&oPponentRigidbody>()
call would return null, and then the rest of the line would attempt to set the
is.inePatic field of null (which isn't possible). Lines like this are not the saf-
est coding practice—so I wouldn't use them in code for a game I intended to
sell—but for a simple prototype, it's usually okay.
2nMouseDoZn() will only be called on the single frame that the player presses the
mouse button down over the Collider component of the Slingshot GameObject, so
this method can only be called if the mouse is in a valid start position within the Sling-
shot GameObject's Collider. An instance of proMectilePrefab is created and assigned
to proMectile. Then proMectile is placed at the launchPos location. Finally, is.ine
Patic on the projectile's Rigidbody is set to true. When a Rigidbody is kinematic, it is
not moved automatically by physics but is still part of the simulation (meaning that a
kinematic Rigidbody will not move as a result of a collision or gravity but can still cause
other nonkinematic Rigidbodies to move).
2. Select Slingshot in the Hierarchy pane and set projectilePrefab to be the Projectile pre-
fab in the Project pane (either by clicking the target to the right of projectilePrefab in
the Inspector and choosing Projectile from the Assets tab or by dragging the Projectile
prefab from the Project pane onto the projectilePrefab field in the Inspector).
3. Click Play, move your mouse pointer inside the active area for the slingshot, and
click. The Projectile instance appears.
